newsitem.title: UK: Argentine convertability plan here to stay - c.bank.
newsitem.headline: Argentine convertability plan here to stay - c.bank.

text.p: Argentina's convertibility plan is here to stay, the peso will not be devalued and depositors can rely on their financial institutions never again to defraud them, the country's central bank president vowed on Tuesday. Argentina has tied its economic fortunes to an inflation-fighting plan of peso/dollar parity engineered by former economy minister Domingo Cavallo in 1991.
Nervousness over whether Argentina would stick to the plan surfaced when Cavallo quit in July, but his successors have sworn to adhere to his reforms.

"I'm convinced convertibility is here to stay, not only because it ensures a stable economic base but also because it is not in the political interest of those who might seek to change the system to alter the rules of the game," Central Bank President Pedro Pou told a London conference on investment in Argentina.
"There is no incentive whatsoever to change such an important foundation of our recently-found stability," he added.

Increased uncertainty since Cavallo's departure has fostered rumours over the future of Argentina's fixed exchange rate system, and analysts at Kleinwort Benson for one say the fixed peso-dollar link is not sustainable over the longer term.
But Pou ruled out any devaluation of the currency.
"There is no possibility that a 15 percent devaluation would improve our economic prospects," he said.

"A 15 percent devaluation would become 150 percent in a matter of minutes and would then cause rapid demonetarisation... and a rapid rise in inflation that would eradicate anything we would gain in competitiveness," he added.

He said Buenos Aires was aiming to become a leading financial centre for the region given the country's size and position in Latin America's free trade bloc Mercosur, and had turned its back on the financial instability of the past that had hurt bank depositors severely.
"Depositors in the financial sector of Argentina have suffered tremendous uncertainty and have been cheated time and again," he said.
"Depositors voted with their feet, or rather with dollars...because the system lacked the essential elements of stablity and predictability necessary for growth."
But he said they should take heart from Argentina's new found ability to resist making them pay in times of trouble, as its restraint during Meixco's "Tequila crisis" showed.
"Our commitment is that we will not defraud depositors ever again," he said.

Efforts to tighten up the financial sector mean banks are now more highly capitalised. He said they were unlikely to face a run on the banking system like their 1994-95 experience when Argentine deposits plunged 18 percent in four months in the aftermath of Mexico's shock devaluation.
He denied criticism that convertibility spelt inflexibility.

"We probably have more flexibility with regard to external shocks than we had before convertibility," he said, adding that the central bank's operation as lender of last resort on a temporary basis during the Tequila crisis had enhanced the plan's credibility.
But given a choice between price stability and bailing out the banking sector with an impact on the currency, price stability would win.
"The convertibility law is very clear -- our first and foremost commitment is to price stability," Pou said. --London Newsroom +44 171 5642 2734
